Title: Mars exploration and technological innovation
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
Searching for any signs of living or past life the Mars exploration missions is an ambitious scientific objective.
Consequently the following recursive process is initiated :
the complexity of technical solutions are often in accordance with the ambitions of the scientific goals which involve a huge cost for these missions
the cost is so high that it is necessaiy to maximize the expected scientific return
this can lead to add specifications which could complicate more and more the design process
To make compatible scientific objectives with technical capacities, it is imperative to make a real technological effort, permanently reconciling innovation and heritage. Technological innovation is extremely necessary for the planet Mars exploration missions.

Title: On the NASA Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Near Infrared Camera Multi-Object Spectrometer ( NICMOS) Cryogenic Cooler (NCC) in a microgravity environment
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract: The NICMOS instrument on-board the HST requires an active NICMOS Cryogenic Cooler (NCC) to replace expended cryogen in order to sustain and extend the operating life of the instrument. The NCC design utilizes three turbomachines, including a compressor in the main refrigeration loop running at over 420,000 rpm during normal operations. The sensitive pointing platform of the HST requires a pointing error contribution from all disturbance sources of no more than 7 milli-seconds of arc (mas) for no less than 95% of any given orbit. Modal contributions from the telescope platform in sensitive frequency regimes require NCC contributions fall into the micro-gravity regime for an acceptable result. In order to design the appropriate experiment to quantify these disturbances, three important issues addressed were the measurement system, an experimental environment that would not contribute to the error in the measurement and finally an experimental design that realistically depicts all operational scenarios of the NCC.

Title: Power system options for European contributions to a future manned Mars mission
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
This paper gives an overview of the European Space Agency’s technology development aims for a future human Mars exploration mission, and particularly emphasises power systems. Static and mobile mission elements selected by a mission architecture study are outlined. The difficulty in generating power for large static mission elements such a propellant production plant using solar radiation is explained, and contrasted with an alternative, a compact, light nuclear reactor. However, arranging the shielding of a nuclear reactor before startup may prove to be a difficult logistical problem on Mars.
Fuel cell power sources for mobile mission elements such as a small long range robotic exploration rover and a large, mobile pressurised laboratory have been modelled parametrically using spreadsheets. The difficulty in storing hydrogen and oxygen in compact form leads to large mass and volume requirements, up to 40% of the mobile mission element total mass.
A brief overview of suitable chemistry for reliable, power efficient propellant and life support consumable resource production (ISRU) on the Mars surface has been given. ISRU plant energy needs are expected to drive static power system design for a future human base, so an accurate system level power estimate is being researched. An inventory of relevant technologies has been commissioned which will enable ESA to focus its technology development resources at an early stage and enhance Europe’s industrial capabilities within human Mars exploration scenarios.

Title: Telecommunications and navigation strategies for Mars exploration
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract: We examine, from a multimission program perspective, key issues and recommended strategies for three aspects of telecommunications and navigation support to future Mars exploration missions. First, we address the challenge of ensuring high-rate, robust telemetry during critical mission events, such as Mars Orbit Insertion, En- try/Descent/Landing, or Mars Ascent Vehicle launch. Obtaining real-time telemetry during such critical mission events, with the bandwidth required to characterize engineering system performance, will provide the program with needed feed-forward information in the event of an anomaly. In addition to quantifying supportable data rates, we will address the mission design issues involved in ensuring communications link availability to an on-orbit relay spacecraft at the epoch of the critical event. Second, we discuss the longer-term telecommunications support of surface assets over their mission lifetimes. The anticipated Mars mission set includes a diverse set of in situ spacecraft, ranging from large, highly mobile rovers with considerable landed mass and power, to small, extremely energy-constrained scout- class missions with little or no direct-to-Earth communications link capability. Telecommunications performance will be quantified for a variety of relay orbit options in terms of such key figures of merit as data return, link availability, and link energy efficiency. Third, we examine the potential for extracting navigation information from these in situ radio links. Specifically, we quantify the navigation accuracies that can be achieved for such program mission scenarios as approach navigation (for aerocapture or precision landing), surface position determination (for highly mobile rovers), and orbit determination (for support of on-orbit rendezvous with an orbiting sample canister).

Title: Commercial Development of the K-1 Vehicle Structures
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: Standard launch vehicle structural component development, verification, and qualification is typically performed under strict control through government or military regulations. When developing a launch vehicle in a completely commercial environment, this history is challenged. In fact, to design, manufacture, and qualify the components of a commercially developed launch vehicle under a system involving serial engineering and manufacture, full-scale static test articles, retesting of supplier-verified components, and other historical practices is fundamentally prohibitive, from both a cost and schedule standpoint. Kistler Aerospace Corporation has taken a new approach to the development of its K-1 Reusable Aerospace Vehicle. Through innovations and new applications of proven techniques, Kistler has addressed the challenging funding and schedule constraints that are inevitably associated with a commercial venture. These approaches to design and manufacture, as well streamlined verification and qualification, are a necessity for success in the commercial launch vehicle industry.

Title: DEVELOPMENT AND UTILIZATION OF THE APM LOGISTICS SIMULATION MODEL (LSM) FOR RESUPPLY DEMAND AND SPARE ANALYSIS SUPPORT
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
The Attached Pressurised Module (APM) constitutes one element of the European contribution to the International Space Station (ISS) programme. The APM, whose operative life will be 10 years, is presently scheduled to be launched and docked to the Space Station in early 2003. The APM project is developed according to the European Space Agency (ESA) requirements.
The Columbus Logistics Simulation Model (COL LSM) has been developed in support of the APM design. The COL LSM satisfies the logistics needs for a statistic tool to analyze support needs of the APM module during the E phase and to compare the results against the design requirements and constraints. To meet this result, the COL LSM provides reports and graphics related to maintenance, parts transportation and storage, Logistics Availability, resupply demand. These projections are derived from a collection of statistics rolled-up from Montecarlo simulations. In addition, the COL LSM capability to release outputs at equipment level offers a valid support to the Spares Assessment and Recommendation process through the performance of a sensitivity analysis aiming to optimize the operational availability of the equipment. The COL LSM constitutes, together with the Columbus Logistics Support Analysis (COL LSA) Support Record System database, an integrated software platform to support the development of the logistics analyses. The COL LSA database, through an interface report, imports in the COL LSM the pre- processed data set necessary to perform the logistics calculations.
The COL LSM allows an easy handling of the COL LSA data to enable the creation of equipment hierarchical structures that, together with the logistics scenarios and models created within the COL LSM, can properly simulate the system behavior.

Title: Distributed Interactive Simulation Architectures and System Engineering Innovation
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
Emerging Concurrent Engineering practices are more
and more considered in the Aerospace Industry as
strongly supporting the new business objectives and
the increasing extended international cooperation in
large projects.
While the business-oriented perspectives in Civil
Aeronautics produced insofar a large interest on these
new practices and their deployment in real
programmes was planned and initiated, in Space
Systems engineering only a limited number of
experiments and industrial trials were conducted to
demonstrate how new ways of working and organizing
the project tasks can help in reducing the
time-to-delivery and the overall life-cycle costs.
The moving scenarios in space industry and the
challenging objectives of long-lived in-orbit
infrastructures operational phases are anyhow
pressing for a continuous revisiting of in-place
processes and standards for their optimization
according to assessed business process
re-engineering objectives.
This paper presents the consolidated results of
experiments performed in the last years to exploit the
potential of collaborative engineering applied, in
particular, to simulation engineering.
It was demonstrated that Distributed Interactive
Simulation (DIS) sessions can be effectively
conducted using existing European and
Intercontinental broadband network services,
connecting involved industrial and research sites in Italy, Europe, USA and Russia by Virtual Private
Networks (VPN) on which different Computer Aided
Engineering applications can be operated and shared.
Additionally, Teletesting scenarios were also
demonstrated to assess the feasibility to establish the
on-line cooperation among dispersed teams involved
in time-consuming and complex verification
campaigns. The specific needs of space system
processes were fully considered to consolidate, trial by
trial, the architecture concepts to be implemented to
build-up novel simulation and verification facilities can
take full benefits from these new technologies. The
underlining "visiorf is to extend the use of simulation
during the design and development process to
minimize the need for people displacement during
either engineering or testing intensive tasks and the
number of physical mock-ups and models to be
developed.
Alenia strategic attention has been put in the period
1993-97 on applied research actions in cooperation
with various European and non-European partners
and is now focused on the build-up and set-up of
pre-industrial systems and products. Applications
based on DIS and Teletesting are in particular under
development to support incoming engineering and
operational requirements, as especially addressed to
the ground engineering support for the In-Orbit
Infrastructures. The performed experiments and
on-going developments include the use of Virtual
Reality models in complex Human-ln-The-Loop,
Hardware-in-The-Loop, and Computational
Intensive simulation scenarios. The defined
Architectures are discussed together with their
utilization in the space and ground segment
frameworks.

Title: Exploration Bench-A New Type of Lunar Activity Base
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
In future lunar missions, lunar resource utilization will be one of the most important subjects, because it will be difficult to vitalize future space development activities without benefiting from them. From this view point some planning of lunar evolutionary base have been discussed as an important element of several exploration architectures in early 1990th. At that time Shimizu Corp. also developed a conceptual design of evolutionary lunar base with McDonnell Douglas Space Systems Company.
Those Scenarios of lunar exploration, however, ought to be reconsidered today, because the situations about lunar exploration have been very much changed in these years. The US government is not so interested in lunar base construction, but much interested in Mars exploration. Therefore, their lunar activities will be very much limited in the near future. Japan have planned a series of unmanned missions to survey lunar environment. Europe have also planned some similar types of lunar missions.
Watching these situations, we have to consider the next step of lunar exploration for scientific survey and resource utilization. In this paper we propose a lunar facility concept, ” Exploration Bench”, to contribute commonly to the activities of each individual mission carried out by several organizations. In this concept every lunar mission should be an exploration bench for a future global lunar development. Many kinds of functions in every lunar mission should be networked, including energy supply systems, communication systems, transportation systems, constmction equipment, and so on. Promoting this concept, a virtual lunar outpost can be established.

Title: HAZARDS TO SPACEFLIGHT
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
This is a critical time in the history of human space activities as there is increasing interest in the use of space for terrestrial applications and in the expansion of the space frontier. The hazards resulting from human activity in space, coupled with the intrinsic hazards of the space environment, represent a growing threat for the expansion of the human presence in space.
Radiation represents a primary concern either for manned or unmanned missions. The effects on spacecraft, such as charging and electrical equipment failures can jeopardize mission success. Shielding and Space Weather Forecasting are two mitigation methods that can minimize the radiation effects on spacecraft.
Only 5% of objects orbiting the Earth are operational spacecraft. Detection and data collection methods are developed to know the distribution of debris and to have a statistical sampling of particle fluxes. The ways to mitigate are to protect spacecraft against collisions and to minimize the population of debris.
As for crewed spaceflight, space is a foreign and hostile environment for humans due to radiation, vacuum and microgravity. Moreover, numerous psychological stressors are at work in this environment, which can lead to the development of social and psychological problems.
Because of the difficulty of quantifying space hazards, S.W.O.T. (Strength, Weakness, Opportunity, Threat) analysis is a flexible technique allowing decisionmakers to analyze these four factors to recommend and to mitigate hazards.
Finally, legal and policy instruments are required to facilitate and allow the definition and enforcement of appropriate mitigation measures.

Title: Innovations for Competitiveness: European Views on “Better-Faster- Cheaper”
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia

Title: PAYLOADS FOR CONSTELLATIONS OF COMMUNICATIO N SATELLITES : DESIGN AND MANUFACTURING CHALLENGES
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
The design and manufacturing of payloads for constellations of communication satellites present specific challenges when compared with more traditional geostationary telecommunication satellites. The tradeoffs between mass, complexity and cost are particularly difficult to make. On the positive side, the higher production rates offer a real opportunity for significant reduction of costs and to introduce new concepts for the management of quality and risk. The short development cycles are not specific to constellations since they are also present for the geostationary satellites.
Alcatel Espace has just finished the manufacture and integration of the 56 GLOBALSTAR payloads. For this first generation constellation, conventional concepts have, in general, been applied. The main innovation has been to use the higher production rates to introduce levels of automatisation in manufacturing, testing and integration that have not been used before. The high number of subassemblies manufactured have also allowed the selective introduction of statistical process controls. In this article the GLOBALSTAR experience will be presented in detail.
Beyond GLOBALSTAR, Alcatel Espace is now designing a second generation constellation, SKYBRIDGE. In this case, the higher complexity of the payload places a downward pressure on mass and cost. To meet these challenging mass and cost objectives, new concepts, beyond GLOBALSTAR, need to be considered. Some of these concepts are: the widespread use of commercial off-the-shelf components (COTS); the implementation of design-for-manufacturing, design-for-testing, design- to-cost and design-to-mass concepts; the acceptation of "best practice" suppliers. The paper will analyse the intended benefits as well as the constraints associated with the introduction of these concepts.
The introduction of COTS would bring the biggest payoff in terms of cost reduction but is also the most difficult to implement. Alcatel Espace has implemented a coherent policy regarding COTS that includes quality, purchasing and manufacturing issues. The paper will conclude with a description of this policy.

Title: ROCKET- SPACE SYSTEM BASED ON BALLISTIC MISSILES OF SUBMARINES FOR TROPICAL CYCLONES SOUNDING
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: Some results of system researche and design studies of a rocket space system (RSS) "Volna-TC" based on SLBM SSN-18 for operative contact sounding of tropical cyclones ( C) are presented in this paper with the purpose of detailed study of this phenomenon and improvement of methods of its trajectory forecasting.

Authors: ['A.J. Barrington Brown', 'S.J. Gardner', 'A. Wicks', 'L. Boland', 'E.C. Graham']
Title: THE FEDSAT SPACECRAFT DESIGN
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
This document illustrates the accommodation of
multiple payloads on an extremely compact microsatellite
structure, based on the Space Innovations
Limited (SIL) MicroSIL™ satellite bus. The
satellite defined in this paper is the design for the
proposed collaboration between the Cooperative
Research Centre on Satellite Systems (CRCSS) and
SIL for the Australian FedSat mission. FedSat will
be launched and operational for 2001, in time for
the celebrations of the centenary of the Australian
Federation. The bus is a 3-axis stabilised microsatellite
with a mass of approximately 50-60kg. It
is due for launch into 800km circular low Earth
orbit (LEO). The communications link will be in
the S-band, with the on-board segment comprised
of the SIL S-band communications units and the
ground segment based on the SIL SGS-2.4 low cost
ground stations. The satellite will accommodate
various experiments: A search coil magnetometer
deployed on a 2.5m boom; a UHF Data Transfer
system; a Ka-band communications system;
precision orbit determination using GPS; a high
efficiency solar cell experiment; a high
performance computer system.

Title: THE PRELIMINARY DESIGN OF A EUROPEAN SATELLITE NAVIGATION SYSTEM
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
A joint German-Russian project to design a new generation satellite navigation systems has reached the stage of completed preliminary design of the space segment. In a three years effort the system requirements, the mission scenario, the payload definition, system trails by means of pilot projects and finally the preliminary design of the space platform have been completed.
The proposed system aims at the combined navigation and communication capability to provide traffic management functions for safety critical systems e.g. for air, rail or maritime traffic control. The combination of navigation and data communication capabilities into one satellite system supports the necessary certification of the system for safety critical applications. Furthermore the layout can be optimized by distributing the communication capacity over a number of satellites.
The concept is based on regional systems of satellites in inclined geosynchronous orbits (IGSO), thus it can be initiated as a European-Russian regional system (ENSS) and then grow into a global system (GNSS- 2) by adding an Asian and an American segment. In order to provide a maximum of commonality with present satellite navigation systems it is proposed to use an
overlay on the GLONASS frequencies with a high chip rate. This would provide an accuracy of better than 5 meters from the space segment alone (without any differential augmentations). The data communication for traffic management functions (~ 2 Mbps) would be performed in the S-band, and the required capacity has been analysed. Other value-added services in the field of positioning and navigation have also been analysed and fleet management is an additional application possible by the proposed system.
The preliminary design of the space segment has taken into consideration the use of a new dedicated platform (total mass 681 kg and 868 kW power), and as an option the use of a modified GLONASS- platform as a low cost approach. The navigation and the communication payloads are defined in a preliminary design status as well. For the launch and deployment a PROTON or a SOJUZ launcher can be used for the proposed future satellite navigation system.
For the implementation and gradual build up of the new system various transition scenarios from EGNOS/GLONASS/GPS to the future ENSS/GNSS-2 have been taken into consideration in order to optimize performance and cost.

Title: A COST EFFECTIVE COMPACT SPACECRAFT OPERATIONS SYSTEM, IN SUPPORT TO AN OPERATIONAL ENVIRONMENT
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract: Low mission costs are essential to increase access to space and to enlarge the user community of space related applications. Low costs can only be achieved by taking a system level view, acting on all aspects of mission development, implementation, launch and operations. While on the space segment leading-edge technology is used to provide innovative solutions, the same efficiency approach must be applied to systems constituting the ground segment. This paper presents a high- level technical description of the ESA/ESOC Spacecraft Control Operations Systems II (SCOS- II) system, developed with the main purpose to provide a generic mission control infrastructure. SCOS-II design is characterized by a distributed architecture and by a strong modular approach, together with a high level abstraction of the spacecraft monitoring and control functionality. The result is a system that, by using new generation software development technology and COTS (Computer Off-The-Shelf) products, provides reusable elements across different missions and allows to focus to the implementation of mission- dependent elements. The paper describes how the SCOS-II system has been successfully used to implement at very low cost, the SOHO spacecraft Monitoring System (SOHO-MS) used during the spacecraft LEOP campaign and subsequently during routine operations. The purpose of the SOHO-MS is both to integrate the NASA MCS with an on-line telemetry history retrieval functionality (as it is provided by SCOS-II) and to provide the NASA/GSFC ESA personnel with a monitoring platform independent from the NASA MCS. Finally the paper provides a brief look to the future of the SCOS-II system, with the conviction that innovation and research for better and cost effective solutions are essential in the today space market.

Title: A Technical Overview of the “SunTower” Solar Power Satellite Concept
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
During 1995-1996, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) conducted a far-reaching reexamination of the technologies, systems concepts and terrestrial markets that might be involved in future space solar power (SSP) systems. The principal objective of this “fresh look” study was to determine whether a solar power satellite (SPS) and associated systems could be defined that could deliver energy into terrestrial electrical power grids at prices equal to or below ground alternatives in a variety of markets, do so without major environmental drawbacks, and which could be developed at a fraction of the initial investment projected for the SPS Reference System of the late 1970s.
One of the key concepts emerging from the “fresh look” SSP study is the “SunTower” SPS system. This concept exploits a variety of innovative technologies and design approaches to achieve a potential breakthrough in establishing the technical and programmatic feasibility on initial commercial SSP operations. Capable of being deployed to either low Earth orbit (LEO) or middle Earth orbit (MEO) altitudes and various inclinations, the SunTower concept involves essentially no in-space infrastructure and requires no unique heavy lift launch vehicle (HLLV). The concept, which can provide power to global market places appears to allow up to a factor of 30:1 reduction in initial investment requirements, compared to the 1979 SPS Reference Concept. This paper presents a technical overview of the SunTower SPS concept, including key technologies, sensitivity trades, operational scenarios. Potential non- SPS space program uses of the SunTower concept and related technologies are identified, including human exploration, space science and commercial space applications.

Title: DEVELOPMENT AND VALIDATION OF THE ATTITUDE CONTROL SYSTEMS FOR A SMALL SATELLITE
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
CARLO GAVAZZI SPACE (Milano, Italy) is involved in a commercial telecommunication program, with the prime contractorship of OHB-System (Bremen, Germany), for the development of SAFIR2, a small satellite for low Earth , sun synchronous orbit.
In the frame of the program, the design and the implementation of the Attitude Control Subsystem (ACS), of which CARLO GAVAZZI SPACE is responsible, has a particular relevance. This system combines passive gravity gradient stabilisation with active control based on magnetic coils.
After separation from the launcher, the ACS must prepare the satellite to a correct gravity gradient boom deployment, by the use of magnetic torques generated according to control algorithms implemented in the on board computer. After a rough earth pointing, achieved by the passive gravity gradient torque, a fine control algorithm is implemented, in order to ensure the requested precision of Nadir pointing.
In this phase, full attitude determination is obtained from discrete system estimators, designed from linear control theory and adapted to include non linear effects.
Methods to feed the estimators with interruptible measure information have been developed and tested. This is possible by switching between the three different calculation for the innovations, each of them based on different combination of sensors : magnetometer and geomagnetic field vector, horizon sensor and sun sensors, magnetometer and horizon sensors. In a similar way sensor fault tolerance is also achieved.
The controller design has been done following the classical techniques of state variable feedback based on optimal LQR feedback gain.
The overall ACS design and development life cycle has been performed by exploiting advanced off-the-shelf tools, which have been used to develop and test the control algorithms, simulate the space environment and dynamics, generate automatically the flight code and test the whole system. This design method permits a prototyping approach of the system, furthermore the modularity of the software makes it completely reusable and allows an easy integration with the data handling software.

Title: NOVEL SMALLSAT DEPLOYABLE LENS ANTENNA FOR COMMUNICATIONS & REMOTE SENSING SATELLITES
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
Many SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) and communication spacecraft applications call for a high gain, large aperture antenna. It is desirable that this antenna should stow in a small volume for launch, and have a relatively small mass. CAL Corporation is developing the DDM (Deployable Double Membrane) technology to meet these requirements. A membrane structure stows compactly, but unfurls in-orbit to provide large, approximately plane, aperture surfaces. This paper addresses the r.f. design considerations for a DDM artificial lens antenna. The lens has elements on two radiating faces which are interconnected by 'zoned bootlace1 tranmsission lines. The elements are microstrip patch radiators realised on the membranes as thin metallised areas.
A rigorous electromagnetic model of the DDM lens is described. It has been used to determine optimal pgeometrical parameters for the structure. A DDM antenna can be configured in various ways, and examples will be given of shaped beam SAR, and of monopulse applications. Specific issues discussed are the dependence of gain and scan aberrations on focal length and patch spacing.
For a DDM antenna on a spacecraft, the effects of lens profile distortions due to 'in-orbit manoeuvre' scenarios have been investigated by porting structural model data to the electromagnetic model, to establish the impact on r.f. performance. The results vindicate the rationale of the artificial lens design in that they demonstrate that performance perturbations are insignificant at gain levels of less than 50 dBI. For a 10m. lens, the DDM concept remains viable up to X-band.

Title: RECENT PROGRESS IN JAPANESE SPACE TOURISM RESEARCH
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
Since 1993 the Japanese Rocket Society has been conducting a formal study program to determine how to establish a commercial service providing visits to low Earth orbit for fare-paying passengers. The first phase of the study was completed in 1995 with the publication of the design of the "Kankoh-maru" passenger vehicle. Kankoh-maru is a fully-reusable, single-stage-to- orbit (SSTO), vertical take-off / vertical landing (VTOL) rocket-powered vehicle. The second phase of the JRS Study Program began in 1995 and included estimating Kankoh-maru's development and manufacturing costs, studying its operation from airports and potential business development scenarios, and considering requirements for accommodation facilities in orbit, and safety and regulatory issues. The second phase was completed in 1997 with the publication of two reports on this work. Due to the growing professional recognition of the JRS work, and to the increase in space tourism research activity in other countries, a third phase of the Study Program has now begun.
Kev words: Space tourism, Kankoh-maru, passenger launch vehicle, reusable rocket, orbital accommodation, orbital hotel.

Title: Risk Management for Microsatellite Design
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
It is shown how the methods of risk analysis have been used in the University of Rome micro-satellite program. One of the driving research topics related to this program is the reduction of cost in building spacecraft. The probability risk analysis techniques seem to be a powerful tool in the field of microsatellites design, to outline possible faults. Innovation and limited budget forcing the designer to move in a very “risky” environment can be faced with an as rigorous as possible decision making method.
In our project cost reduction is often attained relying on commercial, not space-rated components, which of course increases risk. This is why the design process should be led by the careful analysis of the risk associated with the selection of components and construction techniques.
In standard applications risk can be evaluated from reliability data obtained in previous and well known similar applications. In our case, for many components, there is a lack of reliability data, due to the obvious missing experience when dealing with not yet space qualified, or even never flown before components. This lack is overcome with numerical simulations and practical engineering considerations, but does not allow a rigorous reliability assessment.
A simple qualitative analysis is used to rank priorities among subsystems and allocate economic resources and development efforts. The main risk source is space radiation effect on CMOS electronic components. Therefore development resources are directed to radiation effect mitigation. A procedure is proposed to lower risk without using space rated components.

Title: Sources of First Soviet Weather Satellite Creation
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
This year, humanity celebrates 40- th anniversary of first satellite injection and CIS scientific community celebrates 35-th anniversary from beginning of near Earth systematic researches under Cosmos program.
In this connection, history of Soviet Weather Satellite System creation represents some interest. Necessity of weather equipment injection into space was obvious in that years Academician E.Fedorov wrote. It is necessary to know atmosphere state over while terrestrial globe for a long time. Only weather satellite surveillance can give such information efficiently and operatively.
. SDO Yuzhnoye was charged in 1961 develop Meteor satellite in composition of Voshod space-rocket complex with SL-8 launch vehicle on the basis of SS-5 military rocket.
Preliminary development of special geophysical, magneto-metrical,
radiometrical and optical equipment which was ingredient of the weather complex, as well as supporting systems for attitude control, attitude control by means of flywheels, solar battery orientation and so on was carried out on Cosmos satellites developed by SDO Yuzhnoye.
All-Union Electromechanical Scientific Research Institute (AESRE), which had neither experience no production base on development of mechanical constructions and aerial systems, was charged with development of Meteor satellite because SDO Yuzhnoye was hardly loaded with development of powerful military missiles and powerful P-56 launch vehicle for Loon program.
As AESRE had no experience, SDO Yuzhnoye and Yuzhny Machine- Building Plant rendered direct assistance in development of design plans and specifications, production forms and records, and operational documentation as well as in manufacturing of body nodes, development of jet systems, assembly and quantitative production of satellites.
Flight tests of single satellites afterwards were competed by creation of continually operated space weather forecasting system.

Title: What Does the First Manned Mars Mission Cost ? Scientific, Technical and Economic Issues of a Manned Mars Mission
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract: In 1953, Wemher von Braun first proved the technical feasibility of a manned Mars mission on principle. In the following decades further investigations concerning the genera! feasibility of such a mission were performed in the USA as well as in Europe especially with regard to a continuation of manned space exploration after the Apollo Program. Beside a wide variety of scientific, technical, political and cultural objectives, special benefit of a manned Mars mission could 1» expected in the field of exobiology: After the discovery in 19% of possible fossile life forms in Martian asteroids, some scientists believe that the complex search for life on Mars should be accomplished by astronauts respectively scientists. The contents of the paper is based on a comprehensive system analysis approach, where different manned Mars mission scenarios are investigated, compared and optimized with the in-house developed software tool FAST (Fast Assessment of Space Technologies). Possible landing sites on Mars and technical requirements, which result from manned missions to Mars of up to 1000 days are also considered. Furthermore, different Earth-Mars transfer trajectories and strategies to get into a Mare orbit, the design of manned space vehicles at subsystem level and a final life-cycle cost analysis with the calculation of development, production and operations cost are included. The investigations show that the total mass of the space vehicle at Earth departure and the total cost can be reduced by more than 50 percent if a low-eneigy Earth-Mare trajectory in combination with an aerocapture maneuver at Mars arrival is selected. However, the roundtrip-time of this mission scenario is about 1000 days. Assuming a project duration of ten years, beginning with the development phase and ending with the return of the six crew members, the annual average cost amount to about $5 billion at a total space vehicle mass in low Earth orbit of approximately 1000 metric tons. Depending on the achieved cost effectiveness for launch and space operations at that time, the total cost of the first manned Mare mission range from $40 to $60 billion (buying rate of 1995). For the scientific operation on the Martian surface (including the required scientific infrastructure) additional cost of 10 to 20 percent are expected. Furthermore, the life-cycle cost analysis shows that a considerable reduction of at least $ 10 billion can be achieved, if habitat modules derived from the planned international space station and existing main propulsion systems (slightly modified) are used. The total program costs of a potential subsequent second Mare mission could be significantly reduced further to only about $20 billion, because the dominating development costs could be neglected.

Title: INTERMARSNET : THE ALTERNATIVE OPTION
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract: The Intermarsnet mission was envisaged as a joint ESA/NASA participation to the international exploration of Mars and the potential ESA contribution to Intermarsnet was one of the five Medium Mission (M3) candidates for selection in ESA Horizon 2000 long-term scientific programme plan. It represented the only network mission in the International Mars Exploration Working Group scenarios. An european alternative option considered during phase A study consists of a Mars orbiter/carrier spacecraft and three identical passive probes. A dedicated Ariane 5 launcher launched from CSG Kourou in the June 2003 opportunity would deliver the composite into a direct interplanetary hyperbolic trajectory to Mars with a cruising time of about 7 months. The orbiter carries the three probes at the vicinity of Mars, delivers them such as they achieve correct trajectory to their selected landing sites, performs the insertion into Mars orbit and ensures the relay of science data from each lander to Earth during one martian year. Because of low cost objective, the design of both spacecrafts is based on maximum use of existing hardware: mainly Spacebus parts for Mars orbiter and Huygens probe elements for probe. The main features of Mars orbiter and probes are described below.

Title: A MOBILE INSTRUMENT DEPLOYMENT DEVICE FOR PLANETARY EXPLORATION
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: Scenarios for the future exploration of Mars, the Moon and Comets include planetary vehicles as a infrastructure for mobility. Their use enables the deployment of instruments both for in-situ measurements and for soil sampling to different locations of scientific interest. This paper addresses design details of an Instrument Deployment Device (IDD), one of the vehicles currently being considered by the European Space Agency (ESA) for these scenarios. The main design goal for the vehicle is to provide the required functional capabilities to explore surface areas in the vicinity of the lander, while achieving a high ratio for payload / vehicle mass, as well as low mass and power budgets.

Title: COIVIPLEX ANALYSIS OF COSIVIONAUTS ERRORS
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: Spaceflights factors may have negative effect on cosmonauts performance and lead to errors in their work. Therefore, working out the methods of the analysis and forecasting of errors is very important for maintenance of efficiency and safety of “crew - spacecraft” system. The methodological approach to the analysis of crew errors is discussed in the present report. The principles of system character of an error, complexity of interrelationship between an error and psychophysiological state of operator, and dependence of psychophysiological state on the environmentalfactors form the basis of the proposed approach. These principles determin probabihstic sense of errors correlation with psychophysiological state. Procedures of cohection and identification of the inflight data about crew errors and cosmonauts psychophysiological state, statictical evaluation of their correlation, and revealing general law- governed nature of this correlation are component parts of the approach. The data about performance and psychophysiological state of crewmembers received through channels of radio, television and telemetrical communication, the data from spaceflights cyclograms, expert conclusions and reports on final results of missions are the primary information. Identification of these data is made by the experts of Flight Control Centre. The results expected to be obtained with use of this methodological approach may be utilized in the practice of the space flight maintenance, cosmonauts training, and maimed spacecrafts design.

Title: MINIATURE, LOW-COST, HIGHLY AUTONOMOUS SPACECRAFT — A FOCUS FOR THE NEW MILLENNIUM
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
NASA is working aggressively toward greatly reducing the life-cycle costs of planetary, space physics, astrophysics, Earth observing, and communications missions. In order to pursue important programs in space and Earth science and commercial applications of space in the twenty-first century, frequent, affordable missions are required. These are enabled through a fundamental paradigm shift in the ways of doing business and the application and validation of advanced technology. Miniaturization of spacecraft and spacecraft instruments leads to lower mass and greatly reduces launch costs. Use of high-level spacecraft building blocks with low recurring costs simplifies spacecraft design and simulation and, together with advanced manufacturing, assembly, and test, greatly reduces development costs. And making spacecraft highly autonomous greatly reduces operations costs. In addition, measures such as targeting appropriate, focused missions and payloads, minimizing spacecraft power requirements, using low-nuclear or non-nuclear power sources, employing onboard analysis and data compression, and eliminating non-cost-effective redundancy can contribute broadly to reduction in life-cycle costs. This paper expands further on these areas and includes specific example spacecraft design concepts, such as the one illustrated at the right, that are consistent with the vision and approach.

Concepts are being developed that help focus technology development on enabling the kind of spacecraft NASA would like to be able to begin flying within the first decade of the new millennium. The objective for these spacecraft is to greatly reduce flight system, launch, and operations costs while improving mission benefit-to-cost ratios — thus enabling frequent/simultaneous flight of numerous spacecraft and, in the process, providing a catalyst for innovation in technology. The approach described in this paper to meet this objective utilizes innovative system design and new technology to minimize cost drivers including communications, power, nuclear material, redundancy, size and mass, and uplink commanding. It employs production and advanced design, assembly, and testing methods to minimize recurring costs, and it selects missions and payloads that are compatible with the cost- reduction objective and approach. The combination of developing the needed technologies and implementing this approach can meet the objective and enable miniature, low-cost, highly autonomous spacecraft for missions in the new millennium.

Title: Meteorological Mars Observations With Microstations Network (MEMOMICRON )
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: A feasible solution to deploy within a limited timeframe a network of microstations for a Mars survey is suggested. The project is focused on the meteorology and dynamics of the Mars atmosphere and is consistent with the contemporary strategy of cheap, fast, and efficient planetary missions with limited objectives. These microstations (meteobeacons) are based on the prototype of meteopackage instruments developed for the penetrators of MARS 96 mission at the Keldysh Institute, Moscow, jointly with the Finnish Meteorological Institute, Helsinki and the University of Colorado at Boulder, that will be significantly improved. The microstations are much smaller, lighter and superior in design to the currently proposed small stations. The basic mission concept involves the integration of directly measured local ground data and atmospheric profiles measured from an orbiter using remote sensing techniques. Conceptually it is similar to what is commonly used in the Earth's meteorology for weather forecasting. The Scientific Rationale and Mission Design incorporating innovative technology for robust design engineering and scientific instrumentation are described. The proposed mission will provide long-term monitoring and a reliable data base on the meteorology of Mars and will provide a key element in the planning for future manned missions. The project will also contribute to the improvement of general knowledge for weather forecasting on Earth through testing common methods and techniques on a global scale in another planetary atmosphere environment. The paper outlines some results of the preliminary theoretical and experimental study involved in the evaluation of the mission profile, scenario and design configuration.

Title: R A -2 R adar Altimeter: Instrum ent Operation Concept and System Performance
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
The European Space Agency (ESA) has awared a contract to DAIMLER-BENZ Aerospace, Domier to fly on ENVISAT-1 mission the Radar Altimeter RA-2 developed by Alenia Spazio SpA.
RA-2 is a nadir pointing pulse limited radar altimeter operating at two frequencies: 13.575 Ghz (Ku-band) and 3.2 Ghz (S-band).
Its key feature is represented by a new on board signal processing algorithm (Model Free Tracker- MFT) able to autonomously detect, acquire, lock- on and track the earliest part of the radar echoes at Ku band from ocean, ice and land surfaces without intermption, irrespective of sudden changes in surface characteristics and elevation.
The radar echo samples collected at Ku-band are processed by the MFT algorithm to adjust the radar resolution and receiver gain to values which allow the proper sampling of the earliest part of the radar echo. Four resolutions are available corresponding to the transmitted pulse bandwidth of 320, 80, 20 MHz and CW pulse.
The radar echo samples at S-band are collected at fixed resolution corresponding to a transmitted pulse bandwidth of 160 Mhz. They are processed on ground to remove from the height measurement performed at Ku-band the bias error introduced by the propagation through the ionosphere. Point Target Responce (PTR) measurements are also collected at every transmission without interrupting the tracking to monitor the variation of the parameters which have been calibrated on ground.
To assess validity of the design, a series of simulation runs over a variety of simulated test scenarios, representing typical operative conditions as tracking over mountains, ice regions, wet lands, have been performed.

Title: System design and operations definition: a structured methodology
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
The design of complex systems and the development of operations during all phases of a project, from the feasibility study to utilisation, requires the capability to maintain the history of the project, to guarantee traceability of originating requirements and project principles, to derive from that the operational scenarios and finally to verify the compatibility with the architecture. In addition, any complex system is functionally and physically characterised by different interfaces: an adequate identification of these interfaces and of the associated system responsibilities can be managed with a structured methodology.
In general, two parallel processes are followed to guarantee the exploitation of a defined project. The first consists of performing functional analysis and developing activity sequences and associated resource utilisation. The second takes care of the definition of the system architecture and its performance. The methodology aims to achieve coherence between operations development and system design. Changes due to requirement modifications, design evolution and operational constraints lead to the need for a flexible, but structured, approach: this has been achieved with a database-oriented approach. The database structure drives the project evolution to reach well-defined goals, each of them verifiable against different discipline requests. Discrepancies can be highlighted, and critical issues identified, solved or justified. The object-oriented database method generates the operations’ products usually required in a project (i.e., scenarios, procedures, timelining, functional analysis and resource profiles). The aim of the paper is to describe the proposed methodology, to show its capabilities and flexibility. Examples of ongoing projects demonstrate the efficiency of the approach.

Title: The Wet Towel Hybrid Propellant Rocket Motor
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: To overcome defects of conventional hybrid motors, a new concept of design is proposed. It is expressed as the title of this paper, in which the liquid oxidizer fills the gap space in the fuel bed consisting of plastic fibers or films. Both HAN and LOX are evaluated as the liquid oxidizer. Since the critical characteristics concern the burning behavior of the wet towel propellant, burning rates of the wet towel hybrid propellants are measured in a pressure range of 0.1 to IMPa by using a specially designed strand burner for LOX base propellants. Striking features in the results of the experiment are the extraordinary enhancement of the burning rate with increasing pressure as well as the pressure exponent larger than 1. Further innovation is necessary for realization of the proposed idea.

Title: VEGA: A NEW LOW COST APPROACH FOR A LIGHTSAT LAUNCHER
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
The modular Vega Launcher Family is being developed for dedicated and multiple launches of lightsats. The concept of Vega most powerful version, the Vega MK3", is based on a three stage design which utilizes solid rocket motors (SRM) for each stage to achieve a low cost family of reliable launch vehicles.
Nominal Vega MK3" payload delivery capability is around 600 Kg to a 700 Km circular, polar orbit. The useful payload accommodation volume is approximately 11 nA The Vega design is based on the well-known and reliable architecture where the three main stages are stacked one on top of another. The SRM cases are fabricated using composite materials based on filament winding technology. The first two stages are equipped with thrust vector control (TVC) systems and the needed electric and pyrotechnic units. The vehicle equipment bay (VEB) is located directly above the third stage and includes the Vega guidance, navigation and control system (GNC), hydrazine attitude control (ACS) system and the telemetry and safety systems. A payload fairing, with an outer 2.4 m diameter, is mounted around and above the VEB.
The Vega launch vehicle family is based on a design- to-cost process, where the cost is the primary driver. Performance is traded with the cost requirements to provide a cost effective launch solution.
The paper describes the general history of the small launcher development in Italy which has led to the current Vega family concept. The current Vega configurations are described with emphasis on the launcher design-to-cost philosophy, performance and safety and operations scenarios.

Title: VISION 2020: A DESIGN PROJECT FROM THE 1995 SESSION OF THE INTERNATIONAL SPACE UNIVERSITY
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: Students from the 1995 summer session of the International Space University (ISU) carried out an exercise to describe and to plan a desirable (from their point of view) future for space activities. The Vision 2020 Design Project utilized a strategic planning technique called Visioning to derive a picture of desired scenarios for space development. The multinational and multidisciplinary group of 60 participants produced a vision of the future where space activities are predicated on the improvement of the quality of life for humankind. Scientific understanding of the universe, expansion of human presence beyond low Earth orbit, and advancement of technology through space exploration are acknowledged but are not considered to be primary drivers for space development. Their focus on building a robust space infrastructure that visibly permeates and benefits the daily lives of all people may signify a generational shift in motivation from the space advocates of the Apollo era.

Title: LOW-COST OPERATIONS APPROACHES AND INNOVATIVE TECHNOLOGY TESTBEDDING AT THE EUVE SCIENCE OPERATIONS CENTER
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
The NASA Astrophysics Program faces harsh realities in the new NASA budget environment. Even though there is an increasing number of successfully operating NASA astrophysics satellites, the Astrophysics Division mission operations and data analysis budget will be decreasing annually over the next few years. As a result the NASA Astrophysics Division must either terminate operation of successful and highly productive observatories or develop techniques for operating satellites at radically lower costs. The NASA Extreme Ultraviolet Explorer (EUVE) astronomy satellite, which is presently operating flawlessly and returning a stream of scientific breakthroughs in the new field of EUV astronomy, is currently slated to be turned off in 1996. The EUVE project has adopted an aggressive plan to find ways of operating EUVE at lower cost. The EUVE project at the University of California, Berkeley (UCB; which has responsibility for EUVE science operations), and Dr. Ronald Poli- dan of GSFC have laid out a new mission operations concept for EUVE that will allow EUVE’s operating costs to be lowered. It will also provide a management experiment and technology testbed to allow NASA to transfer lessons learned and new tested approaches gained from EUVE to other missions. The EUVE Science Operations Center (ESOC) at UCB, has adopted these approaches and is using new operations software that allows semi-autonomous operations to be implemented. Under this plan the ESOC is making a transition from a three-shift, around-the-clock operation to a one-shift, human-tended operation with use of the RTworks artificial intelligence (AI) software package for autonomous operations during the untended shifts. The conversion to one-shift operations was carried out during 1994 and has been accomplished in less than nine months. An autonomous paging system automatically makes telephone contact with remote duty engineers upon detection of anomalies in the telemetry stream so that response to detected anomalies can be carried out. Additional areas of cost reduction include that of the observatory science planning and scheduling and autonomous monitoring and error correction in the communications and ground computer systems. The on-board robustness of the EUVE spacecraft, a Fairchild MMS platform, allows acceptable risk tradeoffs between on-board and ground functions for assuring ultimate health and safety of the spacecraft and payload system. EUVE has been selected by NASA Code X for testbedding of innovative software techniques for cost reduction in the operations of scientific satellites; EUVE is currently collaborating with researchers at NASA Ames Research Center (ARC), the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), and the Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC). Other areas of cost
reduction include testbedding of direct-to-ground communications with autonomous ground stations (EUVE currently uses the Telemetry and Data Relay Satellite System (TDRSS) for all communications), using the on-board global positioning system (GPS) for all orbit determination needs, and streamlining of data delivery to scientific users via the EUVE electronic archive and provisions for remote computing facilities. An additional critical element of the EUVE low-cost innovations is the direct involvement of University of California undergraduate students in all aspects of operations. The EUVE educational outreach program also uses the ESOC as a laboratory for K-12 teacher training workshops. In this paper we describe elements of cost reduction innovation and technology testbedding on EUVE as well as some lessons learned. One of the lessons we have learned from migrating the EUVE ESOC from three to one shift is that today’s AI software allows the design and operation of a fully autonomous EUVE Science Operations Center. We are now developing plans to migrate from one shift to zero shifts. We believe that this will result in a more robust and lower risk science operations concept than the original three-shift, around-the-clock operations. Although we are suspicious of slogans, we believe that this will be an excellent example of “less is more.”

Title: Low Earth Orbit mobile communication satellite systems: a tw o-year history since WARC-92
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
Mobile communication satellite systems have regularly made the headlines of space industry publications in the 1990s. This paper adopts a new perspective—how the systems evolve over time—to describe the main technical features of the two main types:
- big-LEO systems with voice capabilities: Iridium, Globalstar, Odyssey, Inmarsat P21,
- little-LEO non-voice systems: Orbcomm, Starsys.
This approach reveals the considerable changes, even upheavals, that have affected the design of system components. The apparent stability in the designs is due to outside observers gradually and perhaps unquestioningly perceiving the changes. People’s capacity to forget, compounded by the attraction of innovation, may also have a lot to do with it.
We present the likely causes of these changes: regulatory environment, market forces, financial arrangements , being at the early design stage, etc. We also analyze the effects of these forces on the systems, and deduce the general trends.

Title: SMALL - A LOW COST MISSION TO THE MOON-
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
To initiate public and political support for lunar missions in Europe, a small, low-cost mission (SMALL: Small Mission with A Lunar Light craft) is proposed, that demonstrates new technological developments and also provides a visible scientific return. An assessment is made regarding its feasibility and possible goals.
Based on these goals, promising mission alternatives are investigated, which could also contribute to the preparation of a future lunar infrastructure. Considered as typical mission objectives are investigations of volatile components of the lunar regolith in polar craters with a semi-hard impact penetrator, active seismic measurements initiated by a hard impact, optical mapping of the lunar surface at high latitudes, and the determination of ^He-concentrations in the lunar dust.
Along with the programmatic constraints of low-cost and fast realization these objectives call for the application of available but not necessarily fully qualified technologies with respect to propulsion (e.g. solar electric propulsion), subsystems design (low power/low temperature electronics, low mass components) and scientific instruments. Further requirements to meet these constraints are launch as a piggyback payload to Geostationary Transfer Orbit or a similar high-energy orbit and low- cost mission operations (minimization of ground infrastructure, etc.) .
Mission scenarios for lunar orbit and impact are investigated and a spacecraft conceptual design including a preliminary mass breakdown for the options considered is given. Finally, the programmatic aspects of the proposed mission are discussed.

Title: Design and Operation of the Special Purpose Dexterous Manipulator (SPDM): Advancing the State of the Art in Space Manipulator Systems
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
Assembly, maintenance and operation of the International Space Station will entail the most complex operations ever conducted in Earth orbit. Canada is providing a mobile robotic servicing system which will play crucial roles in the success of this endeavour. The flight elements of the Mobile Servicing System (MSS) include; the Special Purpose Dexterous Manipulator (SPDM), to supplement and replace extra-vehicular astronaut activity for maintenance, assembly and payload servicing tasks; the Space Station Remote Manipulator System (SSRMS), for large payload manipulation and crew positioning, the Mobile Servicing Centre Base System (MBS), which provides a platform for operation of the manipulator systems; and the MSS Maintenance Depot (MMD).
The SPDM represents a significant advance in the state of the art in space manipulator systems, it incorporates two seven degree of freedom arms each equipped with a sophisticated multi-function end- effector, a suite of seven camera and light assemblies, accommodations for transportation of SSF replacement parts, a robotic tool set, and a control system featuring force moment accommodation and active collision avoidance capability. The SPDM is relocatable by the SSRMS and can operate either from SSRMS, on MBS, or when attached to a suitable interface on the space station structure. The design of SPDM allows it to be maintained on orbit in the extra-vehicular environment.
The type of tasks for which the SPDM is being designed are unlike any previously performed by a space manipulator system. This paper describes SPDM design, with particular focus on the characteristics of the operations which drive the design, and the features of the manipulator system which enable it to meet these and other requirements. Examples of task scripts are provided including pictorial representations of the operational scenarios.

Title: FAILURE MANAGEMENT ARCHITECTURE AND TECHNIQUES FOR THE MOBILE SERVICING SYSTEM (MSS)
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
The Canadian Space Agency (CSA) contribution to the International Space Station Freedom Program comprises the Mobile Servicing system (MSS). The on orbit robotic elements of the MSS, specifically the Space Station Remote Manipulator System (SSRMS), the Mobile Base System (MBS), and the Special Purpose Dextrous Manipulator (SPDM) are extensively involved in the Space Station assembly and maintenance operations. MSS elements are often used in critical operations involving dynamic manipulator operations handling large payloads. Failures in MSS systems, and Station Systems that comprise the overall end to end control architecture, must be considered. In particular, failures that lead to a hazardous situation such as manipulator runaway, uncommanded motion, and inadvertent release of a manipulator attached payload must be prevented.
The paper describes the end to end control architecture of the MSS on orbit systems. It describes special design features implemented to increase the operational robustness of the MSS and to prevent the onset of hazardous situations due to equipment failure. This includes built in test features, self consistency checking, and computer monitoring features at various levels within the control architecture. Additionally, the paper describes failure management techniques used to ensure that critical missions can be completed, in the presence of failures. This includes cross strapping options between prime and redundant systems, lockout of a failure manipulator joint which allow a degraded but viable mode of manipulator operation, and hot backup capabilities used in time critical operations.
Finally, the paper provides simulation results showing safing responses to equipment failure which would otherwise result in manipulator runaway. Operational scenarios showing alternate modes of operation in the presence of failures are described and pictorially represented.

Authors: ['David B. Weaver', 'Michael B. Duke', 'Barney B. Roberts']
Title: MARS EXPLORATION STRATEGIES: A REFERENCE DESIGN MISSION
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
A year-long NASA-wide study effort has led to the development of an innovative strategy for the human exploration of Mars. A design reference mission (DRM) is advanced that significantly reduces the perceived high costs, complex infrastructure and long schedules associated with previous Mars scenarios. The strategy enhances the mission return, improves the safety of the crew, and reduces or eliminates many of the obstacles associated with conventional strategies. In particular, the Mars DRM supports crews which explore the surface of Mars for nearly 500 days on the first and all subsequent missions, while limiting their exposure to the interplanetary space environment to periods near those of US experience on Skylab and well within Russian experience from Mir. This surface- oriented philosophy emphasizes the development of high-leveraging surface technologies in lieu of concentrating exclusively on space transportation technologies and development strategies.
Thus, the DRM relies on the in-situ production of CH4/O2 propellant for the crew's ascent vehicle and surface mobility, as well as the production of the necessary water and life support gases for the crew's entire surface stay.
By emphasizing a robust suite of surface capabilities and high-leverage technologies, abort-to-the-Mars-surface emerges as an alternative to the traditional trajectory abort options. The DRM, consistent with this risk-mitigation philosophy, employs a single "common" habitat design for use by the crews during the interplanetary transits to and from Mars, as well as to support the crew during their -500 day stay on the planetary surface. As a result of this balanced approach to mission and crew risk, element commonality, and technology development, human missions to Mars can be accomplished without the need for complex assembly operations in low-Earth orbit. Both cargo and human missions are launched direct to Mars with rendezvous occurring on the planetary surface. The associated reduction in total launch mass allows the first crew of six to explore Mars within a total of four launches of a Saturn VH launch vehicle. Continuing missions to Mars can be conducted with only three Saturn VII launches every Mars opportunity (every 26 months).

Title: SPACE TOURISM FOR EUROPE - A CASE STUDY
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract: This paper discusses the long-range perspectives for commercial passenger transportation into Low Earth Orbit (LEO): a European Space Tourism Initiative. Southern Spain is introduced as a potential location for ‘Spaceport Europe’ from which commercial space trips would be conducted. Based on a market model for a thirty-year time span (2020 to 2050), three different market growth scenarios are developed (no growth; low growth; high growth). These concepts introduce a launch vehicle design which comprises the best features of current European launch vehicle projects (eg SÀNGER, STS-2000) that promise a significant reduction in recurring costs. Technological variables of the transportation system and the infrastructure as well as transportation demand trends have been used as input for an integrated operations and cost model. Computer simulation of passenger transport within the given time span produced cost trends which promise specific transportation costs of as low as $60,000 (1990 values) per seat. Admittedly, such cost figures require very high passenger numbers that might be beyond any real demand.

Authors: ['Ulf J. Lindqwister', 'Stephen M. Lichtenfels', 'Edgar S. Davis', 'Harold L. Theiss']
Title: The GPS Topex/Poseidon Precise Orbit Determination Experiment: Implications for Design of GPS Global Networks
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract: Topex/Poseidon, a cooperative satellite mission between United States and France, aims to determine global ocean circulation patterns and to study their influence on world climate through precise measurements of sea surface height above the geoid with an on-board altimeter. To achieve the mission science aims, a goal of 13-cm orbit altitude accuracy was set. Topex/Poseidon includes a Global Positioning System (GPS) precise orbit determination (POD) system that has now demonstrated altitude accuracy better than 5 cm. The GPS POD system includes an on-board GPS receiver and a 6-station GPS global tracking network. This paper reviews early GPS results and discusses multi-mission capabilities available from a future enhanced global GPS network, which would provide ground-based geodetic and atmospheric calibrations needed for NASA deep space missions while also supplying tracking data for future low Earth orbiters. Benefits of the enhanced global GPS network include lower operations costs for deep space tracking and many scientific and societal benefits from the low Earth orbiter missions, including improved understanding of ocean circulation, ocean-weather interactions, the El Nino effect, the Earth thermal balance, and weather forecasting.

Title: A Lifeboat for Space Station: The Assured Crew Return Vehicle (ACRV)
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
This paper addresses the need and programmatic consideration
for a space-based lifeboat to provide the Space Station
Freedom crew with safe emergency return. Scenarios leading
to crew rescue, philosophy of assured crew return, and toplevel
approaches supporting permanent manned capability in
space are discussed. Major drivers and key issues facing lifeboat
designers, including funding implications and resulting
impact on system design, are identified. Programmatic issues
of evolutionary paths and long-term operations, along with
analysis of resulting technical implications, are also
investigated.
Also presented here are predicted rescue needs as a result
of medical emergencies based on historical data for isolated
manned systems on land and water. These predictions are
compared to more limited data for medical emergencies in
space. Probable medical contingencies that would require
immediate transportation of one or more crew members to
a ground-based medical facility are identified. Analysis is
presented of possible emergencies at Space Station Freedom
that would require the immediate evacuation of its crew. Scenarios
and time lines for rapid egress from Space Station
Freedom are also discussed.

Title: ADVANCED TSTO VTOHL REUSABLE ROCKET LAUNCHER - STUDY STATUS
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
In the framework of its effort to assess the trends of future Space Transportation Systems, AEROSPATIALE has built up a methodology to enable fair comparison between reusable all rocket and airbreathing launchers, thus allowing a rational choice for future reusable and low cost launchers.
As part of this methodology, a study devoted to an advanced TSTO, Vertical Take-Off and Horizontal Landing (VTOHL), reusable rocket launcher is performed. The selection of the present configuration was part of concepts trade-offs reported in a previous IAF paper in 1990 (IAF 90-177).
This paper presents the main results of the current investigations performed in the framework of this Advanced Manned Fully Reusable TSTO VTOHL Rocket Launcher.
As cost reduction and safety considerations require abort capabilities of the future manned launcher throughout the entire flight regime, this issue is first addressed. Since a large portion of critical failures might be attributed to the propulsion systems, the design, sizing and operations of the launcher take into account the potential failure of one or several engines of the stages during the powered flight. In that event, recovery scenarios have been investigated and it was determined when the stages could execute return-to-launch-site (RTLS), Transatlantic-Abort-Landing (TAL) or Abort- To-Orbit (ATO) abort modes. The results show that an appropriate combination of powered and gliding phases with limited relaxation on nominal constraints (loads, acceleration, ...) enables the intact stages recovery throughout the flight regime, from take-off to orbital insertion.
Emphasis has also been placed on the global optimization of the first stage to maximize the ascent powered flight capabilities of the launcher and to maximize the first stage transatlantic gliding flight range capabilities taking into account considerations on aerodynamics, thermal aspects, weight, propellants, stability and control (including separation phase). The results of a trade-off study, performed to obtain a lightweight thermostructural concept, are presented. This trade-off included hot versus thermally protected structures.
Material and design options were also explored in this trade-off.

Title: EXPLORATION MISSION TO SMALL BODIES
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
The intersest for small bodies of the solar system has put high priority for missions to asteroids or comets. Over the past few years, the results from GIOTTO, ICE and more recent fly by of GSAPRA by GALILEO on one side, the stuides on VESTA, ROSETTA Comet Nucleus Sample Return (CNSR), and the CRAF project on the other side, contorted the interest, the scientific value, and the technical feasibility of such missions.
Beside the most ambitious Joint ESA / NASA ROSETTA - CNSR mission, four less ambitious missions scenarios have been Identified by ESA as potential back up candidate european missions.
An ARIANE 5 direct escape launch is assumed from the year 2002. This launcher offers a wide set of candidates targets for each mission scenario, some of which by means of gravity assist trajectories. Reasonable launch mass, compatible with valuable scientific package, have been Identified for each scenario, and the corresponding spacecraft design are discussed in term of mass, complexity and technical risks.
The study of these scenarios offers a wide range of opportunities for small bodies exploration with different level of complexity and cost for mlssionsthat could take place in a nera future.

Title: Origins of the mouse proposal
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
The concept of MOUSE [Minimum Orbital Unmanned Satellite of the Earth] seemed a natural outgrowth of high-altitude research using rockets, which began in 1946 at White Sands, New Mexico, with captured German V-2 rockets.
