The initial MOUSE design, as published in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society in 1952, just forty years ago, visualized a spin-stabilized basketball-sized satellite carrying miniaturized instrumentation. The invention of the Bell Labs solar photovoltaic battery in 1954 gave great impetus to the concept by solving the problem of a lightweight power supply. Still, the idea seemed strange to a public that believed in space travel and in huge manned space stations, as described then in popular magazines. Many investigations followed from the MOUSE design, including the first calculations of orbital lifetime and of equilibrium temperature.
To me, the most gratifying outcome was the TIROS weather satellite, whose design incorporated many of the MOUSE features. I had the good fortune to be appointed, in 1962, to direct the conversion of TIROS into the U.S. operational meteorological system for weather forecasting and earth observations.

Title: Space and communications in developing countries
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract: The developments in Space technology have provided a powerful tool for rapidly spreading communication infrastructure, which is vital to the development process in developing countries. Vis-a-vis the particular needs and constraints in developing countries including limitations of terrestrial infrastructure, wide diversity in traffic pattern among urban and rural populations, lack of financial and trained human resources, urgent needs for establishing reliable communications during natural disasters and with remote/isolated locations etc., the full potential of satellite technology is not yet tapped by several countries to meet their vast and urgent needs. The paper is intended to survey the global trends in technological developments and their applications in the satellite communications that are of particular relevànte to developing countries. The response provided by international systems through their programs, the emerging aspects of the regional systems as well as the experience gained by certain developing countries through their national programs in meeting the challenge of rapidly spreading space technology applications in this area are surveyed. Through an exposition of concrete examples of configuration design and technological adaptations which were carried out in some developing countries, the relevance and opportunities of emerging global trends, technological innovations and application possibilities are discussed.

Title: The ITU response at WARC-92 to rapid changes in design and use of communication satellite networks
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
This paper describes decisions
taken at WARC-92 relating to the
fixed-satellite, broadcastingsatellite,
and mobile-satellite
services. These decisions were in
response to a large number of
innovations in recent years in how
satellite communications systems are
implemented and used. The last time
that there was such a review was in
1979 . The Conference made
considerable progress in making the
regulations responsive to these
changes, but much work remains to be
done. This need is indicated by the
new resolutions and recommendations
drafted by the Conference to have
topics reviewed at future
Conferences.

Title: US Space Station Freedom Propulsion System Operations
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract: Operation of Space Station Freedom in Earth orbit requires the installation of a Propulsion System that is capable of performing various rotational and translational maneuvers as the station configuration develops through the assembly process. The operations envisioned for Space Station Freedom have significant influence on the design of the Propulsion System hardware including primary structure, tank configuration and sizing, and thruster selection. Implementation of this design into the flight vehicle requires interfacing the Propulsion System with onboard systems and flight or ground crews. Operational impacts to the Propulsion System design are provided including the differences between the Primary Propulsion System and the Supplemental Reboost System. Each step in the processing of the Primary Propulsion System hardware is described in detail. Reboost modes, altitude strategies, and resupply scenarios are included to demonstrate how the Propulsion System is integrated into the overall utilization of Space Station Freedom

Title: Unmanned Orbital Servicing - From Ground Tests to In-Orbit Demonstration
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
To operate future orbital infrastructure elements, concepts for unmanned servicing have already been elaborated in the past. Nevertheless, orbital servicing will represent a new in-orbit operations task which requires the well-timed development of basic system and operational technologies. Assuming that in-orbit flight opportunities for demonstration and verification of technologies will be limited also in the future, various tests on ground are considered which offer an alternative, feasible and economical way to support technology development.
In 1991, ERNO has initiated a threefold approach towards the development and finally the application of orbital servicing technologies. Firstly, in the frame of a project called USE (Unmanned Servicing Element) the suitability of a ground test bed to verify servicing technologies has been investigated in order to define basic development goals and essential elements of the facility.
Secondly, a teleoperated ORU exchange has been demonstrated utilizing a neutral buoyancy facility. Main objectives of this experiment refer to the development of a practicable and low cost approach for the investigation of operational aspects in simulated weightless environment. Additionally, the design of a technology demonstration element suitable to accommodate in further steps breadboard subsystems is a topic of the demonstration project.
As the long-term goal of these activities, a flight mission called DUSE is defined which shall accomplish the in-orbit verification of basic servicing technologies. As one result, the programmatic analysis proposes the utilization of the Space Shuttle Get-Away-Special Canister for in-orbit transportation of DUSE. The main objective of this mission will be
to demonstrate such essential technologies like RVD and non-destructive inspection.
This paper provides an overview of the ERNO activities in, the field of unmanned in-orbit servicing technology development. A trade-off dealing with the definition of the role of the respective test facilities supports the definition how to achieve maximum test efficiency. The candidate design of the flight demonstrator DUSE is presented which actually serves as the reference for the following development phase. The results of the mission feasibility analysis and programmatic aspects complete the system investigations.

A threefold approach to develop, demonstrate and verify technologies for unmanned in-orbit servicing has been introduced by MBB/ERNO. This approach is based on the utilisation of neutral buoyancy facilities and a laboratory test build-up. The longterm goal of this activities is the in-orbit qualification of the basic technologies inspection and Rendezvous & Docking, which are essential capabilities of a free- flying unmanned servicing vehicle.
Two scenarios have been defined assuming the in- orbit transportation and mission support of the flight demonstrator DUSE by ih&NSTS, repectively the CIS space infrastructure. The DUSE reference design is optimized for transportation by the NSTS GAS Canister and is subjected to minor changes if accommodation on Progress becomes a viable mission alternative.
The advantages of the DUSE demonstrator are low in-orbit transportation costs and the operational capabilities which may be enhanced towards an operational unmanned in-orbit servicing element. The first mission of DUSE is scheduled for 1995/96.

Title: A mobile habitat for early lunar exploration
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract: The analysis and conceptual design of a mobile habitat for the early exploration of the Moon is presented. Conceived as a forerunner to the fixed base, rover operations are described in terms of precursor and ongoing activities. Precursor missions include early science and geological surveys for the siting of a permanent base and can be operated in either a manned or telerobotic mode. During construction and occupation of a fixed base, the rover serves as a tractor/transporter for materials and crew while continuing as a mobile platform for scientific exploration. Requirements and key design features of a Daylight Rover (figure 1) are described. Operating scenarios that incorporate contingencies, day/night excursions and extravehicular activity (EVA) are presented.

Title: Man overboard! What next?
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract: A study was performed in the Virtual Interactive Environment Workstation (VIEW) at NASA Ames Research Center. Simulations were conducted to assess the feasibility, and quantify the fuel and time requirements for a stranded crewperson to return himself to a space station after an accidental separation. A hand-held thruster, similar to the Hand-Held Maneuvering Unit (HHMU) from the Gemini Program was used for propulsion. Thirty different separation scenarios were composed of three separation rates, five initial spin rates, and ability to use an attitude hold mode in a repeated measures design. Statistically significant results were produced by separation velocity. Fuel, maximum range, time to maximum range, maximum axial range, and final axial velocity increased with separation rate. VIEW was determined to be a useful device for simulating accidental separations and a hand-held thruster is a viable alternative for accomplishing a self rescue.

Title: Organizational impediments to the reduction of costs of space programmes
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract: Spaceflight is very expensive, and after 30 years of sustained activity cannot be considered "mature technology". The principal impediment to cost reduction may be organizational. There is evidence that the expectation that Space Programme Costs will be large, and require government support, leads to expensive Space Programmes. Disasters such as the loss of Challenger or flaws in Hubble are major because of the huge investment in the system. Low cost systems would be replaced more readily, and would evolve more rapidly due to accumulated experience. Organizational practices include advancing technology where available technology could be used, co-operative squabbles about "technology return”, micromanagement, inflexibility in design decisions and discouragement of innovation. The per kilogramme cost of Space hardware should be similar to the cost of launch - indicating, for low Earth orbit hardware, costs of about $5000 - $10 000/kg rather than the current $100 000/kg. The paper provides analysis and examples, and suggests the key organizational factors which may have to be changed to improve the situation.

Title: SPDM robot/astronauts comparisons with the respect to space station Freedom operations
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
Assembly and maintenance of the International Space Station Freedom (SSF) will be performed by either Extra Vehicular Activity (EVA) astronauts or by tele-operated Extra-Vehicular Robotics (EVR). The Canadian Mobile Servicing System (MSS) on SSF uses two robotic manipulators, the Space Station Remote Manipulator System
(SSRMS) and the Special Purpose Dextrous Manipulator (SPDM). The SPDM is being designed to perform maintenance tasks on SSF, including the Mobile Servicing System. This paper presents a comparative study of the SPDM and EVA astronaut missions with respect to SSF assembly and maintenance operations.
SPDM detailed assembly and maintenance procedures and their associated task timelines are developed from requirements and preliminary design concepts. These SPDM tasks are compared with EVA procedures and timelines developed by Fisher-Price for the NASA SSF External Maintenance Task Team Final Report.
A SPAR defined Design Reference Mission (DRM) which illustrates the self-maintainability of the Mobile Servicing System (MSS) is included as a specific example. The DRM includes assumptions and a step by step task breakdown with associated timelines. Replacement of an SSRMS Orbit Replaceable Unit(ORU) is used as a representative task requiring planning of precise dextrous operations for both human and tele-robots. Various parameters which will affect overall SPDM or EVA operations are discussed. These discriminators include the logistics of scheduling, storing and handling ORUs, and the necessity of additional EVA aids (fixtures etc.). Variations in resources available such as power and crew member schedulingfor task completion and hazards associated with maintenance tasks are also examined. Fidelity of these scenarios will be analyzed using a computerized simulation, illustrating critical aspects of the DRM.

Title: Space rescue system analysis and design
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
As we move into an era of increasing manned outposts in space, the potential for space rescue contingencies increases. The space environment is not conducive to spontaneous innovation and does not forgive incomplete planning. Solutions for rescue of crew persons in orbit require thoroughly thought out system designs and rescue scenarios. This paper addresses the space rescue issue and presents the insights gained from a recent study of the subject. Lockheed Missiles and Space Company has been involved in studies of crew rescue and return from Space Station Freedom. Aérospatiale has been involved in studies of Hermes and capsule concepts as rescue vehicles. Lockheed and Aerospatiale have collaborated to study the problem of rescue of crewpersons in space. This paper is based primarily on the results of a systems analysis and design study performed in 1990.
Rescue missions in space provide a unique opportunity for international cooperation and collaboration. It was in this spirit that Lockheed and Aerospatiale chose to team to conduct this study.

Title: Design aspects of a rescue system for manned spaceflight
Publication: IAC 1990 congress proceedings, 41st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 October 1990, Dresden, Germany
Abstract:
A new era of Europe in Space is opened, when the space station COLUMBUS will be on operation in orbit, and hence, the need of a reliable rescue system more and more becomes evident. This, nevertheless, ts accentuated by several experiences made by the performance of long duration manned missions. The present paper deals with the design aspects of a rescue system regarding constraints of cost effective operation.
The risks and hazards during the sojourn in space are introduced briefly. Alternative rescue system scenarios are outlined in conjunction with the space station operational capabilities. On that baseline evaluation criteria for the rescue systems are deducted.
It has been analysed, that the largest impact on the rescue system concept traceable is the management of the crew health risk.
Existing rescue system studies are measured and compared mutually by the evaluation criteria. It is demonstrated that the space station crew recovery at nearly any time needs a reentry rescue vehicle, basicly docked at the space station. A lifting body concept evolves as the most suitable design.
Basing on these results existing concepts have been investigated in the present study. By combination of the lifting body concept with those of previous case-studies, like the MBS LB-10 concept, an advanced rescue vehicle is proposed, that is capable to retrieve three astronauts to earth. The peak accelerations during the rentry phase is estimated below 2g. It is designed for hypersonic flight and normal landing phase.

Title: Operations influence on space station freedom design
Publication: IAC 1990 congress proceedings, 41st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 October 1990, Dresden, Germany
Abstract: The Space Station Freedom is the first experience for NASA and its international partners in building a spacecraft that will be operated and maintained over a multi-year lifetime and that will be permanently manned. To ensure it functions safely and effectively, the operations community has become involved much earlier than in previous U. S. programs. This involvement has taken the form of defining requirements and analyzing the configuration, systems, and elements in terms of operations suitability and supportability. This early participation has had many effects on the definition and design of the Freedom Station. Examples of operations participation include the development of various operations concepts, design reference missions, contingency operations scenarios, and assembly operations assessments.

Title: Technologies for aerobraking
Publication: IAC 1990 congress proceedings, 41st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 October 1990, Dresden, Germany
Abstract: Aerobraking is one of the largest contributors to making both lunar and Mars missions affordable. The use of aerobraking/aeroassist over all-propulsive approaches saves as much as 60% of the initial mass required in low- Earth orbit (LEO), thus reducing the number and size of Earth-to-orbit launch vehicles. Lunar transfer vehicles (LTV), which will be used to transport personnel and materials from LEO to lunar outposts, will aerobrake into Earth’s atmosphere at approximately 11 km/sec on return from the lunar surface. Current plans for both manned and robotic missions to Mars use aerocapture during arrival at Mars and at Earth return. At Mars, the entry velocities will range from about 6 to 9.5 km/sec, and at Earth the return velocity will be about 12.5 to 14 km/sec. These entry velocities depend on, trajectories, flight dates, and mission scenarios and bound the range of velocities required for the current studies. In order to successfully design aerobrakes to withstand the aerodynamic forces and heating associated with these entry velocities, as well as to make them efficient, several critical technologies must be developed. These are vehicle concepts and configurations, aerothermodynamics, thermal protection system materials, and guidance, navigation, and control systems. This paper describes the status of each of these technologies and outlines what must be accomplished in each area to meet the requirements of the Space Exploration Initiative.

Title: Analysis and preliminary concept design of a laser propulsion orbital transport system for cislunar space applications
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract: The following paper presents the results of a study project concerning the use of a Laser Propulsion Orbital Transport System (LPOTV) in future mission scenarios. The transportation requirements are based on the construction of Solar Power Satellites (SPS) in the Geostationary Orbit (GEO). A Simulation Model, which mainly consists of a mass, operation and a cost model, compares different missions and propellants. It attempts to optimize the design of the LPOTV by parametric studies of specific transportation cost. Laser power, absorber temperature and initial mass of the flight units are identified as main system parameters. The specific transportation cost between Earth Surface (ES) and Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and production cost for spare parts like engines, collectors and tanks were identified as the the main cost driving factors.

Title: Analysis and simulation of concepts for lunar surface transportation
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
The paper summarizes the results of the author's doctoral thesis. It deals with the analysis, simulation and optimization of lunar surface transportation systems necessary for lunar development now envisaged by the leading space faring nations on this planet. Starting with a systematical approach to define and structure the problem, a model to compare alternative concepts of transportation systems in the frame of three reference lunar development scenarios of different size was established. The alternatives for selected development scenarios were compared on a benefit to cost ratio calculated by a large computer
based simulation model including transportation system design and operations as well as cost and benefit estimations. Simulation results indicate, that for scenarios driven by present known rationales, only transportation systems with low infrastructure requirements such as electric cars with off-road capabilities seem to be effective considering cost or the benefit to cost ratio.

Title: Escape vehicle concepts for manned space stations
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
It is now agreed that the safety of space station crews will require "space station based" escape means.
An interesting solution for such an escape capability is to develop specific, dedicated low-cost Escape Vehicles (EV). The EV chosen concept will be the result of a compromise between programmatics (in this case cost minimization) and safety targets (the purpose is to cover a maximum of emergency situations).
This paper presents the results of an EV conceptual study performed for ESA by an industrial team led by AEROSPATIALE. Starting from emergency scenarios analysis, three EV concepts have been developed :
- "minimum EV": lowest cost and minimum performance .
- "reference EV": upgraded performances allowing for instance better post-landing safety.
- "ambulance EV" : optimized EV for medical emergencies.
The characteristics of these EV concepts are presented at mission and design levels.

Title: Space station FREEDOM: Update of design
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
At the conclusion of the Space Station Freedom systems Preliminary Requirements Review (PRR) in April of 1988, a baseline concept was identified and the preliminary design was initiated. From January 1989 to today, there has been change in program planning within the National Aeronautics and Space Administration in general, and within the Space Station Program Office in particular. In the same time frame, the United States Congress’s approach to reduce the national budget deficits has raised uncertainty in the available funding rate per year.
This paper discusses the system baseline concept which was initiated after the Preliminary Requirements Review. It also discusses studies of various alternate development scenarios which could provide a space station configuration, that meets the design requirements defined in the Preliminary Design Requirements Document, PDRD, at different funding levels and rates. During the Preliminary Design Review the results of these studies will be evaluated and a baseline design, along with a development scenario will be selected, which meets the requirements of the Preliminary Design Requirements Document and is consistent with the resources available.
This paper discusses the. rephrasing of the Space Station Freedom assembly process, to provide permanently-manned presence in space at a comparable time with reduced early year funding; and results in a completed assembly which includes the capabilities expected in the Space Station Freedom. This is accomplished by stepping through rephrased stages of various capabilities and allows manned operation and science activity at the earliest possible date.

Title: A space station crew rescue and equipment retrieval system
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
Exua-Vehicular Activity (EVA) is a vital resource of the Space Station Freedom Program to be used extensively to support user payload operations and space station servicing operations. Current estimates project up to 650 EVA crew hours per year will be required to support initial operations and could increase significantly during growth operations. Thus, EVA will be called upon to perform a wide variety of tasks safely, routinely, and with a high level of productivity.
Although extreme measures will T>e implemented to insure crew safety at all times during routine EVA, contingency scenarios have identified low probability situations where a crewmember or equipment could inadvertently become separated from the station. Equipmentcould become loose during remote handling operations or a crewmember could become ill during EVA and accidently separate from the station.
To provide the Space Station Freedom crew with an added measure of safety against unforeseen events, a Crew Rescue and Equipment Retrieval System (CRERS) was studied for Space Station Freedom operations.
Alternate concepts which could be used to safeguard against the inadvertent separation of crew or equipment from the space station are discussed. Results of analyses are compared and a recommended concept is described in terms of its design features and its capabilities.

Title: Space station FREEDOM operation costs
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
The Space Station Freedom will provide a permanent manned presence in low earth orbit. The Space Station Freedom configuration currently envisioned will have an operational lifetime of 30 years or more. The cost of operating such a facility in space will be significant, especially taken over its whole life cycle.
In order to constrain these operations costs effectively, positive steps are required in the design and development stage. These steps include generation of an operations concept, deriving from the concept a detailed set of operations functions, establishing a cost forecasting methodology for each function or group of functions, acquiring data and employing the estimating methodologies to produce cost forecasts, and feeding these forecasts back into the design process to influence design decisions. These steps are part of an overall operations cost management process for the Space Station Freedom Program.
This paper presents the progress made by the Space Station Freedom Program to date in implementing these steps. Operations functions are described in the context of an overall operations concept. The provisions for operations cost responsibilities among the four partners in the Space Station Freedom Program are summarized. A discussion of cost estimating methodologies is included by major function for Space Station Freedom recurring operations. To complete the picture, a brief discussion of how operations costs impact the design and development process is provided.

Title: The X-20 space plane - Past innovation, future vision
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
In November 1957, the United States Air Force initiated an aerospace project that was one of the most innovative concepts of its day, and also provided an accurate glimpse into the future. The X-20 space plane, known as Dyna-Soar, never reached operational status—it was cancelled in December 1963, before the first prototype was built. But even though the diminutive vehicle never flew, technological advances made during its development laid the foundation for many later manned space systems, including some as new as tomorrow's headlines .
This paper examines both the history and the technology of Dyna-Soar. The space plane's unique design and its proposed missions are examined, along with the ever-changing political, economic and programmatic environments that led to its conception, its long, painful gestation period, and its demise. The X-20 premiered many innovations to solve the challenges of launch, manned orbital operations and re-entry for a re-usable spacecraft. Many of these technologies did not reach fruition until decades later. Based largely on recently declassified material, this paper places Dyna-Soar into a broad historical context as an interesting research vehicle concept from three decades past, and as the purveyor of a technological legacy whose impacts are still being felt today.

Title: The coming revolution in space transportation
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract: A major change in United States space transportation policy has occurred in the last few years. The joint Department of Defense/NASA Advanced launch System program is intended to respond to this change in policy. The program, initiated in July 1987, conpletes Ihase I at the end of August, 1988, and is planned to immediately enter Phase II. The ALS is cost optimized, rather than performance optimized, and will utilize advanced technology and innovative management and design approaches to achieve an ambitious congressionally-mandated cost goal of $300 per pound to low-earth orbit by the year 2005. The technological innovations will directly benefit other United States space transportation programs, such as the commercial programs and the National Aerospace Plane (NASP).

Title: EUMETSAT: Objectives, programmes and future plans
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
EUMETSAT is a new inter-governmental organisation created in 1986 to establish, maintain and exploit European systems of operational meteorological satellites. The organisation consists of a Council, which meets about three times a year, and a small secretariat to conduct the day to day business. The initial programme of EUMETSAT is the continuation of the Meteosat geostationary satellite system developed by the European Space Agency (ESA). Since January 1987 EUMETSAT has been responsible for the funding and overall control of the current generation of Meteosat satellites, although ESA continues to conduct the programme on EUMETSAT1s behalf. The first Meteosat was launched in 1977. The second, launched in 1981, was still in operation more than 6 years later. Three new satellites of almost identical design and an old prototype are being made ready for launch in the coming years. These satellites provide earth imagery at half hourly intervals together with other services and are used extensively for operational weather forecasting.
The EUMETSAT Council has discussed possible future activities and has agreed a long term plan expressing the detailed objectives of the organisation. These will be examined further by the Secretariat to determine if cost effective programmes can be proposed. The highest priority at present is preliminary work on a second generation of geostationary satellites, to replace the present design from the mid 1990's.

Title: On-orbit servicing and cost effectiveness of Columbus polar platform concepts
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
The Polar Platform is an element of the Columbus programme, the European Space Agency's contribution to NASA's International Space Station programme.
This paper reports on a study which has been undertaken in parallel to Phase Bl and B2 of the Platform design, under contract to the British National Space Centre. This contract was led by Logics, with sub-contracts to both British Aerospace and Marconi Space Systems. The platform design underwent a number of evolutionary changes in Phase Bl, due largely to the changing requirements of both ESA. The design baseline for this study has been the platform documented in the Phase Bl, mid-term review (OTR) in January 1986. This platform design had a total mass of 8100 Kg, including 2200 Kg of propellant for orbital transfer manoeuvres, and 2400 Kg of payload, comprising up to 25 instruments.
Launch was planned by NSTS, and for service every 2 years, also by NSTS , over a 20 year lifetime. The paper also includes references to the impact of changing COLUMBUS Programme scenarios during 1986 and early-1987, notably Hermes baseline servicing scenarios.

Title: Remote sensing the land of east and southern Africa
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
The demand for natural resources data, and for the requisite specialized services in surveying and mapping resulted in the establishment of the Regional Centre for Services in Surveying, Mapping and Remote Sensing(RCSSMRS) in Nairobi, Kenya in 1975. Since 1977 a remote sensing programme has been developed to serve some of the regional needs in training, user support and project design and implementation. This programme is now very much concerned with the application of remote sensing to crop forecasting, forest resources mapping, map revision, and other aspects of natural resources data collection and management. This paper examines training, user products and projects in which they are successfully employed.
In many applications, the satellite data are used as a substitute for a map.
This passive function can be exploited to organize existing field survey teams and use them more effectively. Mapping techniques are found to be effective for scales in the range 1:100,000 to 1 million. Large area mosaics provide valuable context for many regional features. For field assessments of crops, forest or other natural resources, the use of satellite images proved particularly valuable, both for field use and for compiling final results.

Title: Spacehab module design project utilizes engineering services for human factors consideration
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract: This paper discusses the use of state-of-the-art computer graphics simulation for the purposes of preliminary product, vehicle and subsystem design and analysis. With the use of flight simulator type real-time computer graphics, a cost-effective and innovative way of designing vehicles, operations and equipment, through providing an environment for the consideration of Human Factors, mechanisms and robotics design requirements, has been devised. Conventional CAD/CAM methods have not to date been able to adequately address these needs. These capabilities allow the rapid development of a computer generated "virtual operating mockup" of a new design and its' alternatives. Formally of Rockwell International Space Station Division; the author initiated a department which pioneered this technology for design. Used in the product development cycle, especially in the preliminary design phases, more configuration alternatives could be analyzed in relation to a broader set of disciplines. Analysis, such as human factors, mechanism and robotics kinematics, previously beyond the scope of these phases, can now be addressed effectively. Properly modified simulation methods, used successfully in the robotics industries, fulfill the “reach" and general articulation requirements for Human Factors analysis. Once developed, the communication of these complex 3-D scenarios becomes a challenge that engineering animation can also effectively answer. Until recently, efficiency in communicating 3-D ideas has always been an expensively solved problem for technical organizations, substantiated by the overwhelming use of physical scale and fullsize models. The SPACEHAB company, manufacturer of a pressurized module which fits in the first quarter of the Space Shuttle payload bay, required low cost design sizing, configuration variants, specific experiment packaging and human operations analysis. Details of the SimGraphics' simulations and methods, which were recorded in real time on video tape, will be discussed.

Title: System concept for wide-field-of-view observations of ocean phenomena from space
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
The Earth Observation Satellite Company (EOSAT) is the commercial operator of the Landsat satellite system, dedicated to remote sensing of the earth from space. The ultimate success of this commercial venture rests not only with the development of the market for existing satellite data, but also with EOSAT's ability to introduce advanced technology and new data to the remote sensing user community.
As a result of market surveys and early tech- \ nical design tradeoff studies, EOSAT has focused on J the Sea Viewing Wide-Field Sensor (SeaWiFS) as a potential new thrust. Current plans are to fly this sensor on Landsat-6 in late 1990. The data from this instruement will be tailored to serve both research scientists and commercial and operational users in the public and private sectors.
■p Specifically, the instrument is designed to provide ocean-color and sea-surface-temperature data, however, EOSAT believes that the data will also be useful for land-based applications. The baseline sensor concept will provide daily coverage (at the equator), 1 km resolution, and six spectral bands in the VNIR and two in the LWIR.
As a result of these early efforts, EOSAT and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) assembled a working group in February 1987 to determine the requirements of the oceans remote sensing user community for a sensor providing ocean data. This working group consisted of scientists and researchers, commercial and operational users, and system implementers. The charter of the working group was to establish end-to-end system requirements for the SeaWiFS mission, specifically defining:
• Science/Research Users' Requirements,
o Commercial and Operational Users' Requirements,
• Sensor Specifications,
0 Data Downlinks and Data Formats,
o Output Products,
• Mission Operation Scenarios, and
• Data-Dissemination and Data-Access Plans.
This paper presents an overview of the results of the working group and current plans for implementation of the SeaWiFS mission.

Title: Holographic interferometry near gas/liquid critical points: Results of Spacelab D-1
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
The Manned Maneuvering Unit (MMU) was designed and built to perform a wide array of in-orbit extra-vehicular tasks. To date, the MMU has flown on three Shuttle missions and has demonstrated the capability to perform just some of its intended missions. During STS-41B in February, 1984, the MMU demonstrated the capability to both translate 91m (300 ft) from the Shuttle and dock with a structure in the cargo bay. The ability to replace the MMU batteries and recharge its nitrogen fuel tanks was also proven by the pilots. Two months later on STS-41C, the MMU flew to the spinning Solar Maximum satellite, matched rates through very precise piloting and attempted multiple docking maneuvers. In November, 1984 each of the two extra-vehicular STS-51A crewmembers flew an MMU to a spinning satellite, docked with it, and nulled the rotation rates so both satellites, the Wes tar VI and Palapa B-2, could be retrieved. In addition to docking with and stabilizing satellites, the MMU was designed to provide a work platform for servicing free flying satellites, to transfer structural members for on-orbit construction, and to rescue crewmembers from a disabled spacecraft. This paper describes methods of on-orbit rescue using the MMU.
Three basic rescue scenarios are presented - rescue of unsuited crewmembers from a disabled spacecraft using the Personnel Rescue Sphere (PRS), rescue of a suited extra-vehicular activity (EVA) crewmember (either conscious or unconscious), and rescue of a disabled MMU crewmember using a second MMU. The PRS is a self-contained, one-man life support system developed by NASA which permits transfer of personnel from a disabled vehicle to a rescuing Orbiter. Crewmembers don the PRS in the airlock and use a portable oxygen system until the transfer to the rescuing vehicle's airlock is completed. The PRS is attached to the MMU arms and a suited EVA crewmember transfers the PRS to the airlock of the rescuing spacecraft. The rescue of a free-floating EVA crewmember, either conscious or unconscious, would be performed in a similar way. The conscious crewmember can tether to and hold onto the MMU structure for the flight to the airlock. An unconscious crewmember would be tethered to the MMU pilot in a manner similar to the PRS. Likewise, the rescue of a disabled MMU follows a similar scenario.
Simulations in the Space Operations Simulator (SOS) at Martin Marietta Aerospace in Denver, Colorado, and the Weightless Environment Training Facility (WETF) at Johnson Space Center, Houston, Texas have demonstrated the feasibility of these rescue scenarios. The SOS is a six-degree-of-freedom simulator for MMU flight which has, among other capabilities, the ability to simulate variations in the MMU/crewmember mass properties and plume impingement as necessary to demonstrate a couple between the MMU and the object being rescued. Results of MMU flights, using mass properties equivalent to those of the rescue scenarios, have indicated that the MMU maneuverability is acceptable for such operations. Crewmembers training in the simulated zero-gravity environment of the WETF and in suited laboratory evaluation have determined which rescue positions are easiest to achieve in terms of handholds and tether attach points. Although more simulations will be required for the development of procedures for a specific mission, the techniques are feasible.
The MMU structure currently has two tether attach points which can be utilized for rescue of a conscious crewmember. In addition, the MMU has the capability for placement of attachment devices on the arms. The actual design of the attachment interface on the arms for the PRS or a crewmember has not been developed; however, the arm interface has been proven for hardware attachment on all three MMU Shuttle flights.
The experience gained on the three MMU Shuttle flights, combined with the simulation results and minor hardware design requirements, indicate that the capability currently exists for on-orbit rescue using the MMU. This capability can be implemented for use on the Shuttle and for future Space Station operations. It is a capability that should be demonstrated during a near-term routine Shuttle EVA mission in order to develop confidence in the system.

Title: Envrionmental control and life support (ECLS) system for space station - No single answer
Publication: IAC 1983 congress proceedings, 34th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–15 October 1983, Budapest, Hungary
Abstract:
As a result of Space Station studies over the past twenty years including the recent studies on "Space Station Needs, Attributes and Architectural Options" [conducted by NASA and supported by many other nations having a strong interest in Space Station technology] Hamilton Standard has concluded that no single Environmental Control and Life Support (ECLS) System is optimum for the wide variety of Space Station scenarios proposed to accomplish the full range of Space Station missions being considered. The payoff for ECLS water and oxygen loop closure is significantly influenced by the cost of resupplying expendables. The cost penalty for resupply is much greater for polar or geosynchronous orbits than for a low altitude near equitorial, orbit. The number of crew members needed to conduct Space Station tasks is another direct influence on the cost trade of open versus closed loop ECLS. The frequency of Shuttle visits to the Space Station further affects the "cost optimum" degree of ECLS system loop closure. For example, the water produced by the Shuttle fuel cells while attached to the Space Station could be transferred to the station, providing a significant quantity of potable water for the station crew, offsetting much of the advantage for processing wastewater into clean water. Scavenged cryogens from the Shuttle's external tank could be brought to the station and used to provide metabolic and leakage oxygen as well as fuel to a Space Station fuel cell (which may exist on the Space Station as a part of a regenerative fuel cell/solar array energy system) producing significant quantities of potable water for the Station crew. Orbital Transfer Vehicle (OTV) operations supported by the Space Station may require large quantities of in-orbit stored cryogens. Even with .advanced insulation concepts, the cryogen boil-off could provide metabolic and leakage oxygen as well as fuel for a fuel cell providing potable water. These Space Station operational considerations, coupled with an in- orbit evolutionary station concept, starting with a relatively simple two or three module station with a small crew and growing to a large station complex with many crew members and even several Space Stations in various orbits indicate that no single ECLS system solution is optimum for all applications. It is important that many system
concepts be available when a specific mission design scenario is selected. Subsystem technology options should be pursued to support these various system alternatives so that an adequately mature inventory of ECLS approaches exists for the various Space Station scenarios. The system technology activity should also include evolutionary ECLS systems concepts which support an in-orbit growth capability without discarding equipment used in early ECLS system configurations. This paper discusses ECLS systems configurations which may be used with the wide range of Space Station scenarios. Supportive subsystem technology is also discussed.

Title: Design to life cycle cost capability of the PRICE models
Publication: IAC 1982 congress proceedings, 33rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  27 September–2 October 1982, Paris, France
Abstract:
PRICE is a family of three parametric cost predicting models, currently widely used in U. S. government and industrial circles. A number of European organizations also use the PRICE models.
A case study, utilizing the PRICE Hardware and Life Cycle models, is here presented to illustrate the cost impact of maintainability considerations for Avionic equipment. The study depicts a tradeoff analysis to assess the economic impact of designing equipment with two different technologies for changing deployment scenarios.
This case study is not intended to provide a definitive answer on the level of technology to be employed in the design of avionics. Rather, the purpose of this analysis is to illustrate the flexibility and utility of parametric estimating models. Through the use of these parametric models, a practical method now exists to conduct multiple, rapid, design-to-life-cycle-cost trade-off analyses.

Title: Impact of space development on educational motivation
Publication: IAC 1981 congress proceedings, 32nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 September 1981, Italy, Rome, Italy, Italy
Abstract:
The paper addresses a systems approach to education designed to help prepare for the fourth environment. The systems approach builds on the interacting and interdependent resources for innovation found in 1) Academia, 2) Industry, and 3) Government.
The systems approach was the basis for the design of a course in Space Development which is now in its fifth year. The objectives of that course were to 1) Promote awareness of, as well as develop a knowledge-base in, the many subsystems which must be considered in Space Development (e.g., physical, psychological, and social subsystems), 2) Research the interrelated issues of hard and soft technologies, and 3) Contribute to an ongoing analysis of Space Development issues from a systems approach. The paper summarizes how those course objectives were attained, as well as the new options in education and professional career goals which have developed for students subsequent to the course.

Title: The Tiros era - 1960-1980 and the decade ahead
Publication: IAC 1980 congress proceedings, 31st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  22–28 September 1980, Tokyo, Japan
Abstract: The TIROS Meteorological Satellite system has provided global weather observations since April 1960 for the U.S.A. and the world community. In the past two decades, the TIROS polar-orbiting satellite has progressed through four generations of design. The TIR0S-N/N0AA configuration is the present operational system. The Advanced TIROS-N is under development to enhance the system with additional pay- loads for environmental observations and the search-and-rescue mission. The operational products from the TIROS/ESSA/ITOS/NOAA* family of satellites have been routinely applied in weather forecasting and have been beneficial to mankind.

Title: Orbit transfer needs of the late 1980s and the1990s
Publication: IAC 1979 congress proceedings, 30th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  17–22 September 1979, Munich, Germany
Abstract:
Early high-energy payloads will be transferred from Shuttle orbit to higher orbit by using the expendable Inertial Upper Stage (IUS) or the Spinning Solid Upper Stage (SSUS). Later, the advanced payloads (which are yet to be fully understood by spacecraft designers) will require a more sophisticated Orbit Transfer Vehicle (OTV) with higher payload capability and possessing a high level of orbital operational flexibility.
Orbit transfer requirements will extend from synchronous equatorial to planetary orbits and perhaps beyond. Manned as well as unmanned operations are anticipated. Multiple Shuttle flights may be necessary, and the advanced spacecraft are likely to be transferred from Shuttle orbit to high earth orbit (HEO) in the form of separately transported modules which rendezvous and are mated at their final destination. Some payloads will place certain restrictions on the transfer vehicle, such as maximum thrust/weight (T/W) or minimum transfer time.
Mission scenarios are outlined which include selected examples of advanced revolutionary spacecraft. Spacecraft modularization policy is a key element in .the definition of mission requirements, and it is crucial to adopt a coordinated approach to spacecraft and OTV design.
In addition to transferring primary mission payloads, the OTV will have to perform many sophisticated support functions, such as rendezvous and docking, orbital maneuvering, servicing, retrieval, and the transfer of man. The complexity of space operations is expected to mandate space facilities that support the primary missions, such as power modules and space assembly/construct!on facilities. These, if required to operate at higher than Shuttle orbit, become themselves candidate OTV payloads. The additional requirements that are imposed on the OTV are considered along with those imposed by the primary missions.

Title: United States manned spacecraft reliability experience
Publication: IAC 1974 congress proceedings, 25th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  30 September–5 October 1974, Amsterdam, Netherlands
Abstract:
Completion of the Skylab Program on February 8, 1974, signaled the end of the fourth major U.S. manned spacecraft program and the thirtieth manned spacecraft flight. More than 7000 hr of manned flight commencing with Project Mercury and extending through the Apollo Program were accumulated. The experience gained from the four major space programs in little more than 15 years provided the impetus for formulating the reliability approaches being used in the present Space Shuttle Program.
Two key spacecraft design guidelines were used to the degree practicable in Project Mercury, which was the first manned space-flight project. They were: (1) no single failure shall cause an aborted mission, and (2) no single failure during an aborted mission shall result in loss of life to crew members. Use of proven components was emphasized in Project Mercury spacecraft design. A requirement existed that all failures and anomalies would be resolved before space flight.
Approaches similar to the project Mercury reliability controls were used in the Gemini Program spacecraft, which were two-man spacecraft used to conduct research in rendezvous techniques. Basic design changes that enhanced reliability based on Project Mercury experience were made in the Gemini Program.
The Apollo Program (U.S. manned lunar landing missions) was designed using a number of key design and assurance principles derived from previous manned spacecraft program experience. Because the command module spacecraft hardware was essentially the same for the Skylab Program (with some modifications), the design and assurance principles were complied with fully for the Skylab Program. Additional testing was necessary to ensure confidence in the longer-duration Skylab missions. Reliability practices for experiments required some revisions or tailoring because the loss of a single experiment did not mean the loss of a major mission objective.
Specific reliability disciplines have evolved from previous spacecraft programs, and these disciplines currently are being applied to the latest U.S. manned space-flight program, the Space Shuttle Program, which involves a reusable orbiter vehicle. A summary of the major reliability tasks and innovations being used on the Space Shuttle Program is presented.

Title: The Post-Launch Performance of the Tiros I Satellite
Publication: IAC 1960 congress proceedings, 11th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1960, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract:
TIROS I is the first of the experimental television-equipped meteorological satellites to be launched in the TIROS program of the U. S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration. The satellite contains two television camera systems—one wide angle and one narrow angle (high resolution) for photographing the earth’s cloud cover from an altitude of 400 nautical miles.
The camera outputs are transmitted to earth-based stations, where the video data is recorded on tape and also presented as a conventional TV picture on a kinescope display, and photographed. Operation of the picture-taking equipment can be controlled directly from an earth station, or indirectly by means of stored programs, sent to the satellite to initiate an operational sequence at a later time. Other equipment carried includes telemetry, satellite dynamics stabilization devices, a solarcell power supply and auxiliary systems for identifying the location on earth of the pictures taken.
An elaborate ground complex supports the TIROS I operation. Primary ground stations for commanding the satellite and receiving data from it are located in Hawaii and New Jersey. Tracking is done by the Minitrack network. Facilities of the U. S. Weather Bureau, Navy, and NASA in or near Washington, D. C. are coordinated for processing returned cloud pictures and satellite orbital data, and preparing the programs for future picture taking.
The performance of TIROS I in orbit is still being evaluated. The passive thermal design has proved quite successful, as has camera coverage and resolution. The power supply has proved more than ample, and radio communications have been reliable. The function-controlling clock of one camera system went out of operation for several weeks, but has returned to a satisfactory status since then. The attitude of the satellite’s spin axis has changed at a greater rate than had been expected. Analyses of these latter situations are still under way.
TIROS I has proven extremely valuable as a meteorological research tool. Large area weather systems have been photographed and identified. Both known and apparently new cloud and weather phenomena have been observed. Meteorologists are striving to recognize the limits of the present design and the direction for future improvements. There now seems little doubt that satellite meteorology will become an established branch of weather research and forecasting.
